podcast.body: Recorded in the midst of the Watergate scandal in 1974, this upbeat funk dance song subtly critiques Richard Nixon and the government. While its lyrics are less biting than other protest songs of the era, they directly express public fatigue and dissatisfaction with political leadership, such as "We are sick and tired of hearing your song telling how you are going to change right from wrong." The song reached number five on the charts the week ending October 5th, 1974. Stevie Wonder intentionally crafted a catchy, lighter melody to embed a heavy message, believing people are more likely to listen and think if entertained. "Stevie said that was the point he said quote the best way to get an important and heavy message across is to wrap it up nicely"

This 1974 chart-topper was an "unabashed rant" against President Richard Nixon, released just weeks before his resignation following the Watergate scandal. Wonder made it clear that Nixon was the explicit target of the song. "Like Stevie Wonder's 1974 chart-topper, you haven't done nothing. An unabashed rant against Richard Nixon just weeks before he resigned the presidency following the Watergate scandal."
